svg.aria-label: Diagram: how AWS Glue Schema Registry compatibility modes encode a deployment order, and what each one covers. The upper half sets out the direction each mode assumes. BACKWARD, the recommended choice, lets consumers read the current and the previous schema version and is used when deleting fields or adding optional fields, which assumes consumers upgrade before producers. FORWARD lets consumers read the current and the subsequent version and is used when adding fields or deleting optional fields, which assumes producers upgrade first. FULL covers the previous or next version but explicitly not earlier or later versions. The ALL variants, BACKWARD_ALL, FORWARD_ALL and FULL_ALL, check against all previous schema versions rather than only the adjacent one. NONE accepts any new version without a compatibility check, and DISABLED prevents new versions entirely. A middle panel records the consequence of pairwise checking: a run of individually compatible changes can leave a recent version unreadable by a consumer several versions behind, because each step only ever compared against its neighbour. The lower half records the counter-intuitive JSON rule: adding an optional property under BACKWARD registers only when the previous schema set additionalProperties to false, and is rejected when the previous schema set it to true, because old data may already carry that property name with a different type, so a permissive schema cannot later make a claim about a field it previously allowed to be anything. A closing note records that the checkpoint determines which version new versions are checked against, and that editing the schema definition or compatibility mode in the console moves the checkpoint to the latest version by default.
svg.title: Each compatibility mode is a promise about who deploys first
svg.text: “Compatible” is not a property of a change
It is a property of a change relative to a deployment order — and the mode is where you declare which.
BACKWARD
— AWS’s recommended choice
Consumers read the current and the previous version.
For deleting fields, or adding optional ones.
Assumes: consumers upgrade first.
FORWARD
Consumers read the current and the next version.
For adding fields, or deleting optional ones.
Assumes: producers upgrade first.
Both check one neighbour — FULL covers “the previous or next version, but not earlier or later versions”
So a run of individually compatible steps can leave v6 unreadable by a consumer still on v2, with every step having passed.
BACKWARD_ALL / FORWARD_ALL / FULL_ALL check against all previous versions. A replay consumer is always behind.
The JSON rule that inverts the instinct — adding an optional property under BACKWARD
additionalProperties: false → accepted
additionalProperties: true → rejected
Because if the old schema allowed anything, old messages may already carry that property name at another type —
“for example string instead of number.” Declaring it now contradicts data that already exists.
And the baseline can move without anyone deciding to move it
The checkpoint is the version new versions are checked against. “In the console, editing the schema definition or
compatibility mode will change the checkpoint to the latest version by default.” No failure, no warning.
An open schema feels future-proof. It forfeits your ability to say anything definite later, because you already promised the field could be anything.
Constraints are not the opposite of flexibility here — they are what preserves it.
